titel: Your first order at a US broker
kurz: Which five details determine the price of an order at a US broker, and why the largest cost item does not appear anywhere, even with zero commissions.

bloecke.md:
An order is an offer to enter into a contract, even if it is sent at the push of a button. It consists of five details: which security, what quantity, on what condition, how long the offer is to remain valid and at what time it is sent. Unlike in many European markets, US brokers usually decide themselves where an order is executed; the time of day and the order type are the levers that remain with you.

The commission gets talked about the most, and at most online brokers it is $0 for US stocks and ETFs. The execution price, by contrast, does not appear as a cost item in any breakdown. It results from the time of day, the order type and the liquidity of the security, and it is the cost that remains when the commission is zero.

schritte.text: Take the ticker symbol and, if in doubt, the CUSIP from the fund company's website or the company's investor relations page rather than from the search results. Check share class, whether it is an ETF or a mutual fund, and for foreign companies whether it is an ADR.

Trade during the regular session from 9:30 to 16:00 Eastern Time, and avoid the first minutes after the open, when spreads are often still wide. For ETFs with foreign shares, the morning hours, while European exchanges are still open, are often the cheaper time.

Enter a number of shares or, where the broker offers it, a dollar amount for fractional shares. If you calculate the number of shares too tightly, the order can be rejected for insufficient funds if the price rises.

schritte.titel: Set the order type and limit
schritte.text: When buying, set the limit just above the ask price, and when selling, just below the bid price. Use market orders only for very liquid securities during the regular session.
The most sensible setting is “Day”. If the limit is still to apply the next day, set it again in the light of the new prices instead of leaving a good-'til-canceled order in place for weeks.
The preview shows the estimated amount, the commission and, for sales, small regulatory fees. It does not show the spread, because it is contained in the price.

Compare the execution price with the bid and ask you saw for the same minute, check the number of shares and report anything unusual to the broker immediately. Since May 2024, US stock trades settle one business day after the trade (T+1).

bloecke.md:
## Ticker, CUSIP and ISIN

In the US, securities are found by their ticker symbol. It is short and convenient, but it is not unique over time, and similar tickers belong to completely different products. The unique identifier is the nine-character CUSIP. The [[International Securities Identification Number (ISIN)|ISIN]] of a US security consists of the country code US, the CUSIP and a check digit. The country code stands for the jurisdiction of the security, not for the company. An S&P 500 ETF with an identifier beginning IE… is therefore an Irish fund and, for US persons, a tax problem rather than a convenient alternative.

The most common source of error with a first order is searching by name. Under the same index name you will often find several ETFs from different providers, a mutual fund with several share classes and different fees, and leveraged or inverse ETFs whose names differ only by a word such as “Ultra” or “2x”. Some companies have several share classes with different voting rights and tickers. With foreign companies, an [[American depositary receipt (ADR)|ADR]] with its own ratio and fees often appears instead of the share. In the search results, these entries look almost identical.

bloecke.md:
In the US, a share is traded on more than a dozen exchanges and many alternative trading systems at the same time. The best bid and best offer across all exchanges form the National Best Bid and Offer (NBBO). Regulation NMS prohibits executing an order at a worse price than one displayed on another exchange. Most retail market orders do not reach an exchange at all: online brokers route them to wholesale market makers, which execute them from their own inventory at or better than the NBBO and pay the broker [[Payment for order flow|payment for order flow]] in return.

Outside the regular session, there is no such depth. In the pre-market and after-hours sessions, few participants trade, and a single order can move the price. Many brokers therefore only accept limit orders there. With an ETF that holds foreign shares, there is an additional factor. In the US afternoon, European and Asian exchanges are closed, so the fund's holdings are not traded, and the market maker has to estimate their value. It demands a wider spread for this uncertainty. The [[Indicative net asset value (iNAV)|indicative net asset value (iNAV)]] helps as a guide, but during these hours it is itself based on last prices from closed markets.

bloecke.titel: Price certainty and execution certainty of order types
bloecke.unter: Schematic. The top right corner remains empty, because price certainty and execution certainty pull in opposite directions and every order type demands a choice between them.

felder.text: Execution practically certain, price open. Justifiable only for liquid securities during the regular session.
There is no order that guarantees both execution and price. With a limit, the price is secured, but execution is not.
The market decides whether the order is triggered and at what price it is then executed.
Price limited, execution uncertain. The sensible standard case for private investors.

bloecke.md:
A [[Market order|market order]] means immediate execution at whatever price is available, not at the best price. Most brokers display only the best bid and offer (Level I). The order is executed against these and, if the size there is not enough, also against offers at worse prices further down the order book, which can only be seen with depth data (Level II). This is why large market orders in thinly traded securities become expensive.

A [[Limit order|limit order]] sets a price limit: a maximum price when buying and a minimum price when selling. The drawback is that execution is not certain. If the order is also meant to be executed, the limit belongs just above the ask price or just below the bid price, and not 2% away from the market. Execution is then very likely, and the protection against outliers is still preserved.

The minimum price increment matters too. For stocks above $1, the quote increment for most stocks is one cent. For a $10 share, a one-cent spread is 0.10% of the price; for a $500 share, it is only 0.002%. Low-priced shares are therefore relatively more expensive to trade, even when the spread is as narrow as it can be.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation: a purchase at the ask costs half the spread compared with the mid price. With the same spread in cents, the cost in per cent falls as the share price rises.

bloecke.md:
A stop order does not guarantee a sale at the stop price. When the price touches the stop, it becomes a market order and is executed at the next available price. If a share opens 20% lower after a profit warning, it is sold at the bottom of the gap and not at the stop price.

On 6 May 2010, the S&P 500 fell by a further 5% to 6% within around four minutes, and the Dow Jones at times by more than 9% (around 1,000 points). Between 14:40 and 15:00 New York time, around 2 billion shares changed hands. Triggered stop orders were executed at prices that were no longer being traded minutes later. The regulators responded with [[Circuit breaker|circuit breakers]]. Market-wide trading halts now apply when the S&P 500 falls 7%, 13% or 20% from the previous close, and the Limit Up-Limit Down mechanism pauses trading in a single stock for five minutes when its price leaves a band around its recent average. On 24 August 2015, many ETFs nevertheless traded far below the value of their holdings in the first minutes of trading, and stop orders were executed at those prices.

A stop-limit order does limit the execution price, but in a crash it may not be executed at all. It therefore replaces one risk with another. Many brokers also do not trigger stop orders outside the regular session, or only on request.

## Time in force and partial execution

The time in force is the detail that is least often set deliberately. A day order expires at the end of the regular session to the extent that it has not been executed; for extended hours, brokers offer separate settings. A good-'til-canceled (GTC) order stays in place until it is executed or cancelled, at most brokers up to a maximum period, often several months. A limit order that sits in the order book for weeks is an open offer to the market. If bad news arrives at some point, this order is the first to be executed.

If there is not enough volume on the other side at the limit, a [[Partial execution|partial execution]] occurs. With commission-free trading in US stocks and ETFs, this hardly costs anything extra. It does where a commission applies per order or per execution day, for example for options, broker-assisted trades or foreign shares. Where the broker offers it, the condition all-or-none (AON) ensures that the order is executed only in full.

Fractional shares and orders in dollar amounts are convenient, but many brokers execute them only at set times or as market orders, and some do not accept limits for them. For larger amounts, an order for whole shares with a limit is the more controllable route.

In an illustrative calculation, an investor invests $2,000 in a large US index ETF at 14:00 Eastern Time. The bid price is 99.99 and the ask 100.01. This corresponds to a spread of 0.02% (2 basis points).

- When buying at the ask, the half spread relative to the mid price costs 0.01%, that is $0.20.
- The commission is $0.
- Together this comes to $0.20.

If the same order is placed at 7:30 in the pre-market, where the spread is assumed to be 0.20%, the half spread costs $2.00. Both trade confirmations show the same commission of $0. The difference of $1.80 does not appear anywhere as a cost item; it only shows up in the worse purchase price.

With twelve such purchases a year, that amounts to $21.60. Measured against an annual investment of $24,000, this corresponds to 0.09% and thus three times what an index ETF with an expense ratio of 0.03% costs on the same sum in the same year ($7.20). And this is solely about the time of day.

bloecke.md:
With bonds, you order a face value instead of a number of units, and the price is quoted as a percentage of face value. An order for $3,000 face value at a price of 96.40 costs $2,892, plus [[Accrued interest|accrued interest]] for the period since the last coupon payment. The quoted price is the clean price without accrued interest; the settlement amount corresponds to the dirty price. That is why the amount debited is higher than the price alone would suggest.

Most bonds are traded over the counter with a dealer acting as principal. The dealer's markup is contained in the price. For many retail trades in corporate and municipal bonds, the confirmation must show the markup or markdown (FINRA Rule 2232 and MSRB Rule G-15). US Treasury securities can also be bought directly at auction through TreasuryDirect, without a markup, in amounts from $100.

An executed trade is final. A cancellation because of an obviously wrong price, a clearly erroneous execution, must as a rule be requested from the exchange within 30 minutes, and only if the price deviates from the reference price by more than set thresholds, for example 10% for shares up to $25 during the regular session. If the trade confirmation is only read at the weekend, the deadline has long passed.

Good-'til-canceled and stop orders usually do not rest at an exchange; the broker holds and manages them. How a broker treats them on ex-dividend dates, after stock splits or other corporate actions differs; some adjust them, others cancel them. A limit that is to remain in force should be checked after such events.

The standard order for private investors is a limit order during the regular session. Market orders are the exception and are suitable only for very liquid securities at times when many participants are trading.

- A **fill-or-kill order** (FOK) is executed immediately and in full, or not at all.
- With **immediate-or-cancel** (IOC), as much as possible is executed immediately and the rest lapses.
- With **all-or-none** (AON), the order is executed only in full, but it may wait.
- The **one-cancels-other** combination (OCO) links two orders so that execution of one cancels the other, typically a price target and a stop. A **bracket order** combines a purchase with such a pair.

Which of these conditions are available depends on the broker and differs considerably between app-based and online brokers. Investors who need them should check this before opening an account.

mitnehmen: An order consists of five decisions, and with zero commissions, the cost lies in the combination of time of day, order type and liquidity.
Execution certainty and price certainty are mutually exclusive; the sensible standard case is the limit order during the regular session from 9:30 to 16:00 Eastern Time.
When triggered, a stop order becomes a market order and does not protect against price gaps; a stop-limit replaces this risk with the risk of non-execution.
The same spread in cents costs more in per cent the lower the share price; outside the regular session, spreads are considerably wider.
The trade confirmation should be checked right after execution, because clearly erroneous trades must be reported within minutes; US trades settle on T+1.

begriffe.text: National Best Bid and Offer: the highest bid and lowest offer for a security across all US exchanges. Under Regulation NMS, orders may not be executed at worse prices than those displayed.

Combination of a stop price and a limit price. When the price reaches the stop, a limit order is created instead of a market order. It protects against execution at outlier prices, but in a crash it may not be executed at all.
Stop order whose stop price follows the price upwards at a fixed dollar or percentage distance and stays put when prices fall. Once triggered, the order is executed at the next available price.
Mechanism that pauses trading in a single US stock or ETF for five minutes if its price moves outside a band around its recent average price. It prevents executions at outlier prices.
Trade at an obviously wrong price. Exchanges can cancel it on request within short deadlines and only above a minimum deviation from the reference price.
